title: Mike Rutenberg & Byron Storer Press Conference | October 29th, 2026
text: You gradually narrow down that group, and then you determine, well, these are the guys who will be your short kicker replacement, long kicker replacement, and retainer replacement. And then, usually, your replacement kicker and your punter swap places , you know what I mean? But that's something that, you know, every week we have a field goal blocking period, and that's the time when our short kicker and retainer replacements practice. And then, during our emphasis period on punting return today, our long kicker replacements also get reps. So, the guys know, Corey and Dray, they know they have to make a couple of punts and a couple of field goals every week to make sure that, if we find ourselves in that situation, at least they 've done it a couple of times during the week. One of the guys in the injury unit who does a lot for you, Winston Reed. He also made a great play in that goal-line defense.  Do you feel a little bit of pride when your guys get those opportunities and manage to make plays like that? Absolutely, you know, I'll take complete care of Winston Reed. He's definitely 100% our special teams man, but, you know, what we want for all these players now, and their dreams maybe aren't to enter the NFL thinking, "My dream is to play special teams in the NFL ."  I mean, it's a great way to make a living now. But you know, you always want to help them develop their talents, and that one day they'll have the opportunity to go and play on defense or offense and become starters. So, you know, we're just trying to help develop our guys, and hopefully they'll have a mindset of being ready for the next step, so that when they're called upon, they're ready to step in and play defense.  And it has happened now.  Many guys, the longer you stay in this league on special teams, get injured, and then they end up becoming starters at some point. It's just that it's special teams, if you're a good special teams player , you're going to be in the league a long time and you're going to have opportunities to make plays on defense or offense, you know? What about the fact that Andre, Corey, and Rex, the ending between this game and the Baltimore game was so similar, there was even a missed field goal at the beginning of the fourth quarter? On the last kick, a guy gets ahead and you have to readjust, and the way they handled everything was similar to what happened two weeks in a row.   I know.  Yes, it was very, very similar. Um, I think in this one, having gone through the previous one, we were a little, you know, the group in general, we were a little fresher. They were a little more frustrated because Dre comes out there and knows he can land that kick, so I feel like his competitiveness comes out in that situation. He's more upset and angry about missing that kick, but I know he has the ability to reset. They have a very good support system between the three of them and were able to regain their composure, get out there and have the cunning in that situation to repeat our signal so that they ended up getting ahead , so they didn't block another field goal , and we ended up advancing 5 yards to kick the winning goal a little closer. So, in general, I could tell that Dre was frustrated because he would have liked to get the first one in. But then he came back with a great mindset and the boys stayed calm and handled the situation better than the previous week. So, overall, it was good. Good ending, but you know, when the game was over the four of us got together and said , you know what? We need to make things a little easier for ourselves from now on .  That's how it is. Any particular reason.  I know Dylan said after the first game back that we saw him make a kick return earlier in the season. Is there any reason why he didn't do it in this first game back? Is it something he might get back into as time goes on? Yes, Dylan is one of our best kick returners. But I always want to put someone who is 100% healthy and 100% fresh. So I'm just letting him get back into the swing of things , get some more practice, and hopefully at some point we'll have him back in the game. But I'm not in a hurry to, you know, put someone there who isn't 100% healthy, or you know, only when he feels safer. The offside that moved Andre at the end.   You know, I was talking to Andre after the game and he kind of hinted that it was something Corey did. Mhm. So, they are trying to measure the time of the check-out count.  How often do you guys work on that? And how do they have different variations of that to help achieve it on game day, I suppose? Well, we're always... You're speaking from the perspective of a field goal, right?  To combat that.  Do they practice changing...? The cadence? The cadence so that yes, as if that allows it to happen or causes it to happen. Yes, we are definitely constantly working on our cadences because we understand that people do that not only in game situations, but in normal situations.   You know, if they feel that, well, coaches like me, assistant coaches like me, are studying our center and our bra, and they feel that they are consistent, that they do the same thing over and over again, and they feel that they can look at the cue instead of the ball to gain an advantage.  That's a big advantage for them. And that's why we combat that by working on our double flash cadence or different things we can do to make sure we're aware that we're being watched. But, in general, I don't necessarily love that rule of allowing these guys to jump offside like that . I think there's a risk of someone getting injured, and you'd hate to see them jump offside on purpose and someone get hurt.  Now you have your substitute kicker trying to score the winning goal.  I just don't think that's what the NFL wants.   Do n't they have, I mean, do they have an automated quarterback for the defenders? Would you favor something like that, where both have the deadlock as soon as they jump? Yes, I think there must be a better way because, you know, it's been two weeks in a row that we've encountered the same situation. The first time they blocked us, the second time we got ready.  Well, there was a time when I was with the Raiders in 2021 against Dallas and coach Vassell did it three times in a row. And so, you know, for me it's that we have to be careful in that situation to make sure, I'd rather not see anyone get hurt in that All good? Perfect. Very quiet.   I'll ask you this question. Slow starts, you know, obviously are n't what you guys want to do. Are you noticing things like, maybe not schematically, but something, you know, a sort of common thread in the way they've started, like they did in Tennessee and others, that you can, you know, is there a sort of common thread with that, about why the beginnings are the way they've been? In everything we do.  And you said it, of course, we don't want to allow a touchdown on the first series.  We don't want to allow a touchdown on the fifth series, or on the eighth series. In everything we do, if it doesn't meet our collective standard, we address it head-on as a group and work to the best of our ability to fix it. In everything we do, when it meets our collective standard, we are constantly trying to improve it. So, whether it's the first series, something else, something we're doing really well, it's a constant building throughout the week of the why, telling the truth, trying to work it out together and really pushing ourselves to fix it.  And it's a really great process, collectively, as staff and players. What have you been able to identify as the problem?   I'm going to keep everything we identify internal, but what I can tell you is: whatever is going on within the defense, and Monk does a great job within the team, whatever is going on, all we do is try to find that advantage, try to find one more way we can improve and help the football team win.  And if there's something we didn't do to our standard , here's how we can fix it immediately to help the team win. It felt like there were so many different ways the defense stepped up and answered the call—by themselves, by the offense, by the special teams. Whether it's the defense on the goal line, Denzel's interception, and then the forced fumble after...In those moments, I know it's something like bang, bang, bang. But what are those conversations like when they know we've allowed this to happen, whether at one stage or another , and we have to give a response?   It all comes down to our defensive style: playing for each other, enjoying it to the fullest, playing intelligently, doing our duty , playing aggressively, and going for the ball.  So, when things are going well, it's a constant reminder: let's maintain our style, style is above scheme. Let's make sure we do our job, play with everything, with aggression, and attack the ball.  When things aren't going well, there's no magic potion.  It's about continuing to give our all on the field.  Hey, let's celebrate the good stuff.  Let's fix what's wrong quickly.  Ah, let's get on with our task .  Are we playing aggressively? Let's go for the ball.  It's that constant defensive approach: whether it goes well or badly, we're always going to go for it. It's a credit to our team in all three phases, but defensively speaking , our resilience and never- give-up attitude are a credit to the players. They are the ones who do it. I believe that in that series, on the third down play, Aiden Huntington was tackled and he described to us how he quickly got up to make the play What does that play at that moment say about Aiden?   I'm speechless, because what is n't it saying, right?  That's everything he stands for .  That's everything our defense stands for.  That's everything our team stands for.  And that's how we all deal with things.  And at that moment, he did it.  They knock him down and he gets up again. Carson, or rather Mason, is stretching. Nine other colleagues are doing everything they can to fight.  He gets up and, collectively, we make a play to help the team win.  But again , it all comes down to the people we have in our defense and on our football team.  And when they're between the touchlines, giving everything they have until they can't anymore.  That was the epitome of it all.  As for Aiden, he does it every day in training. Regarding that defense of the line, I mean, in general, going from thinking they were going to allow another touchdown and that it ended up resulting in a 14-point change, but getting that stop after they nullified the touchdown, does that exemplify everything you've been preaching to these guys since you arrived? Well, I don't want to take credit for what I preach.   It simply exemplifies who we really have. And who we are as a defense and who we are as a football team. And regardless of the circumstances, we're going to do our best.  We're going to try to do our job as best as we can and play with all the intensity we can. It shows that these kids keep going, keep fighting, and if you get hit, you hit back. It's what we believe in on defense, it's what Monk preaches as a team, and it's what we do every day, but it all starts with how we come together. We conduct our meetings in the same way.  How do we do the routes? How do we practice? How do we study?  And then, with luck, you get your reward.  At that moment they gained it because of who they are. title: Offensive Coordinator Bobby Slowik meets with the media | Miami Dolphins
text: Good job, obviously last Sunday. The coach mentioned his play selection, and I know it's always about the players and that you would praise them, but I wanted to ask what you think changed last week, whether it was more distinct run formations that you think made a tangible difference in the game. Yes, I mean, we really did rotate the staff a bit.  I know we had a little more, I wouldn't say it was a huge amount, but we added a little more here and there. Honestly, we approach the week in exactly the same way as the rest of the year. There's a lot of what we do now where we try to find different ways of doing the same thing and packaging it differently, you know? For our boys, we have a youth group.  So the more repetitions we can get doing repeatable things, the more we want them, and you can't just line up and do things in the NFL the same way over and over again .  That's a recipe for disaster.  So we spent a lot of time trying to change some appearances about how we do the same things. And make some things look the same and add a detail here or there that's a little different, you know?  And that was mainly the whole game plan , whether it was related to personnel, it could be 21, 12, 22, 11. Part of it was related to formation, action, passing, you know , we just wanted to vary things . But at the end of the day, the boys came out and that was, by far, our best-executed game;  They simply played very good football, and that will always be the starting point. And regarding Willis, were the passing plays you called as the primary option designed to get him to release the ball more quickly than in previous games? Yes, I would say there was definitely an intention against certain formations they had where we knew we were going to have to get rid of the ball quickly and give it away quickly.  In particular, if they put pressure on us, they forced us to act quickly or left some empty areas in their zones, and it turned out that we took advantage of some of those early, at the right time.  And Malik did a great job of being in tune with the skill players, the eligible players, and the receivers, making that happen.  So, uh, yeah, I would say there was definitely an intention to do that. There were other plays where, you know , we were trying to advance the ball up the field and we didn't get a clear view, and he was very keen to just hand the ball over, move on and go to the next play.  So I thought he really took steps forward in his confidence about what we're doing and how we're doing it. Now, obviously, every week you spend in the NFL, the defensive schemes and structures change drastically, you know?  So, last week it was very difficult to advance the ball up the field and we knew it, and this week is a totally different situation in terms of how they want to outline and organize things. So, you know, we need the same confidence and conviction against the Patriots this week. After deciding to go for that final fourth down and one yard, are there any other plays that even come into consideration?  In other words, does it matter if they know what's coming? Will it simply be a surprise play to win the game? Yes, I think a lot of that has to do with the kids you have, the culture you have, you know?  Our guys, as soon as Half was talking to the offensive line, they said, "Yeah, let's go."  "We're going to get this done and win the game."  And then I came in and said, " Hey, here's the situation."  "Here are our options."  "What do you want to do?"  In other words, they didn't even blink.  And at that moment, as the person in charge of calling the plays, you think it's an easy job, you know what I mean?  And I think everyone has a lot of confidence in that play, and that fits perfectly with the style of football we want to be a part of, you know? So I think for us at that time, it was an easy decision on my part and it was a lot of fun to watch them execute it the way they did.   It's called an analysis table.   I have her right in front of me.  It is an analysis table.  Who knows?  But he says you are, by far, the one in charge of calling the least predictable plays in relation to down and distance, series after series and game after game Um, I don't know if you saw the chart, is that something you really want to be in that top corner for? And is there any way you can get to that top corner ? Yes, I think that's fascinating.  I didn't even know there was a way to track that or predict something like that, you know? Uh, I've told you before that the starting point for me, as the one who decides the plays, is always to do everything possible to keep the defense unbalanced.  Now, I think we need to take all of that with a grain of salt.  For example , if every time it's second and 14, just because you don't want to do what everyone else does and throw the ball, you run with the ball 100% of the time, you're not going to win any games.  Do you know what I mean? But there's definitely a part of making sure the defense is never sure what they're going to get, while you do the things you know you do very well. And my staff has been incredible.  Halfley has been fantastic in helping me, and all of us just coming together to find different ways to combine things or put together plays that we think can keep the defense off balance.  I think we've really taken a step forward in our third-down running game this year, compared to any other offense I've been in.  You know, I think that's been very important for us. And really, to bring that to every part of our offensive.  Yes, that's important to us. What will he learn about his rookie receivers after his matchup against Christian Gonzalez? Uh, you know, I hope I don't learn anything I don't already know .  Do you know what I mean? I think our young receivers are all talented. I think everyone is very competitive, and I think everyone has that competitive spirit to rise to the occasion, you know? So I would really be surprised if I came here after the fact and felt something different than that. Now, that doesn't mean they're all going to go out there and have 100 yards and receptions;  Gonzalez is a very good player, you know?  He might be having a really good day, but we're going to compete.  And in that, I am as confident as I could possibly be in our boys.  Since they're going to compete, we're going to give it our best effort. Obviously, that fourth and one after the two-minute warning is the play everyone is talking about because it sealed the result, but it wasn't the first time you guys took a fourth down in that game So I just want to talk about the style of American football they try to establish by being aggressive in those opportunities. Yes, I mean, fourth down decisions are primarily made by the head coach , you know what I mean?  And I'm more in communication with him just to make sure I have a play ready, you know, when the situation arises.  From time to time he'll say, "Hey, are you okay if we do X, Y, or Z?" But most of the time, that's entirely up to him and our game situation manager. Uh, but we talk about it a lot because we know we want to be aggressive when we have the opportunity to score .  That's our big focus right now .  We don't have many possessions per game, so we want to make sure we finish as many as we can with some kind of points. And taking a chance on the fourth opportunity is a very important part of that.  So we've talked about having plays for that .  Uh, and probably the most important thing for me is communication with the quarterback in those situations, you know , I thought when we advanced on fourth and two, uh, I think that was an incredible play by Malik.  We had a play that we liked, uh, in the aerial game.   We did n't win the one-on-one on the front side completely, so he had to progress to the back side.  And as soon as he progressed to the back side, he saw a window and an open running lane, and simply took the opportunity and ran.  And you need that kind of conviction on fourth down in this league, we got like four or five yards on that play, and he made it pretty easy. Uh, and that's really the most important thing for us.  Having such confidence and conviction in the plays we ask for at that moment where we still put them in good positions to win, and they can execute so quickly. And then I think we're going to succeed What things did Caleb Douglas do right afterwards? He competed very hard, you know? I think he plays with attitude and determination. I think all receivers do it;   It was one of the most physical matches we've ever had.   I do n't know what they showed on television, but when I saw the tape, our receivers were fighting on the field We were sending some guys to the ground.  We were fighting right up until the final whistle.  They wanted to go out and compete. They wanted to fight for every play. Caleb proved it every time;  I think it's a big step for him because he has it inside him. And he's at his best when he plays that way. He's a really talented route racer I think that part comes naturally to him.  He has very good footwork. It has a huge reception range.  His first touchdown, I mean, was an awesome route, you know?  It's difficult for anyone to cover that up.  So that part, I think we always know will be there.  It is that intensity, competitiveness and physicality that I believe he still wants to develop further. I know that sometimes you want the boys to get off to a good start.  You want the players to get into a rhythm during a match. Others see it that way too.  We'll throw the ball where the defense doesn't want us to throw it.  With Chris Bell, did you go into last week thinking you wanted to involve him? Yes, I honestly think it's a bit of both.  Probably for everyone in the NFL.  Do you know what I mean? You generally go into a game with plays in mind for everyone who's going to contribute to the offense, and you try to make sure you distribute them in some way, usually in the first half. I think it's something common for most people.   It's not...it's much harder than it looks to make that work in the NFL .   Do you know what I mean?  So I was glad that Chris was able to make great plays, like that third down catch that was key for us down the sideline on an out route. He made an incredible play on a screen pass.  You know, I think those are the easy plays where you just think about putting the ball in his hands. Screens are an easy way to do it.   We did n't block particularly well on that play.  He simply evaded three people and gained us eight or nine yards.  So, I was very pleased with how he played. We're going to continue doing the same thing we 've been doing.  Do you know what I mean?  We'll try to make sure everyone gets the ball and, hopefully, at the right time so that everything goes But the most important thing for all of them right now is that they are playing the game the right way.  When you do that, it's just a matter of time. What do you think Jerry Kingston has done well during his time here? Yes, well, it's still a bit of a new face for me.  Do you know what I mean?  He's been working with the offensive line guys for a while.  He is putting in his best effort in individual work.  I saw him a little bit in the practice team at first.  He has made great progress in terms of committing to what we teach and do in terms of fundamentals and technique, which is very different from where he comes from. And it wasn't an easy transition for him. So I think he finally feels secure about that. When he came in against Cincinnati, we strongly believe that the next man should be ready, but at the same time Cincinnati has a very good front line, especially in the interior. And you never really know how that's going to turn out.  We finished the game and, generally, I did n't realize Jared was in the game.  Do you know what I mean? Which is a good thing when it comes to an offensive lineman.  It's a very good thing when the person calling the plays never realizes it.  I thought he put in his best effort when he watched the tape, and I think that gave him a lot of confidence.  Because he has simply moved on.   It has been on the rise ever since, which has been fun to watch.  So I'm excited that she has this opportunity. The closed wing was used a little more last week. Was that more because of the opponent? Or was it more of an understanding that it has been one of the underutilized positions until now? Uh, yeah, no, it usually depends more on the opponent, you know?  We are a team of 21 staff members and that, again, is really not going to change for us. We want to move the ball.  We believe in running the ball, and one of the easiest ways to attack a defense in today's NFL is to have someone in the backfield who can get into different areas.  That's not common anymore. So people find it hard to adjust to that, you know? Now, that doesn't mean I don't like using Personal 12, you know? When it fits, when it works, and when we believe our personnel have an advantage over theirs, we'll make sure we have those plays to include, mix it up, and balance the passing and running a bit, but it depends a lot on what we're seeing. Last question about his offensive versatility.  I believe you had scoring runs of three, seven, 14, and 15 plays. They had a 91-yard drive, scoring by air, on the ground, with the running back and with the quarterback. Is that significant when you're evaluating attacking versatility, or is it just, well, that's football? Yes, no, for me it's a very important issue.  Being able to score in many different ways is the starting point for scoring consistently, and I think we all know that's something we 've been working on: putting points on the scoreboard more consistently. We took a big step in that direction Personally, I love series where we are on the field for 14, 15, 18 , 19, 20 plays.  They give me a headache , but they help the team a lot when you have series like that that end in points But the reality is that if you want to score a lot of points in the NFL, there will be series of only four or five plays where you connect with explosive passes and make big gains downfield. So, being able to do both, taking advantage of both. I think right now we're very good in the first one, in the long series part I think we need to increase our ability to capitalize on explosive opportunities for the remainder of the season. And we have a new face in the building What can you tell me about your interactions with Christian Haynes, and, you know, what do you like about him? Yes, I mean, I've seen it on video. Um, we've really only said hi so far , you know what I mean?  So , I haven't really had to talk to him much yet.  He came in full swing with the offensive line trying to catch up on a lot of things.  Uh, yes, we have a similar scheme to the one he came from in Seattle.  It's not so different , uh, from what Flurry does up there .  So, there is some familiarity. He just plays the game the way we want it played, you know?  He is a good American football player.  He plays hard, he plays physical, uh he can move people around in the ground game.  It has been solid in its protection.  It's like he goes, he plays with a lot of effort and strength.  These are the things that matter to us and that we want to represent, and I'm excited to see, you know, how far it goes here in Miami.

title: 😮The 49ers TRADE Arms Race just expanded to the whole NFC…
text: I was going to lead with potential wide receiver trades for the 49ers, Garrett Wilson and others. In fact, that was the topic of conversation as I was driving in Tennessee not too long ago, but the Chicago Bears just traded with the Tennessee Titans. Funny that I was in Nashville for Jeffrey Simmons, all prodefensive tackle. The arms race in the NFC is fully on. The arms race has now grown from the NFC West to the NFC as a whole. Remember when the Bears played a week ago on Thursday Night Football against the New England Patriots? And the takeaway was that Caleb Williams is super impressive. He's actually number one QBR.1 points ahead of Brock Birdie who's number two. But the takeaway was that the Bears defense is not good enough to contend. They rank number 16 in EPA per play. Well, the rage now in the NFL is to go out and get a dominant interior pass rusher. The improvement efficiency might be the best out of that position. And I by that I mean if you get one of these guys like the Bengals got Dexter Lawrence, the 49ers have obviously gotten Osa De Gazua and now DeForest Buckner and now the Bears are getting Jeffrey Simmons. If you get one of these guys, it's what will most efficiently and quickly elevate your defense because quarterbacks, even the mobile guys, struggle to get away from interior pressure. The Bengals, for example, they were the number 29 defense in the entire league last year. They traded the 10th overall pick, a firstrounder for Dexter Lawrence. I know that's not the only move they made, but it's the key move that they made. They're the number five defense so far this year. From number 29 near the very bottom to top five. The 49ers went from 56 combined pressures from their defensive tackles to Osa Deazua for a third round pick. That's 51 pressures all on his own last year. plus now divorce Buckner for a fourth round pick. Now the Bears, they're spending a whole lot more. Two first round picks and a fourth and it's a fourth fifth swap, but essentially two ones for Jeffrey Simmons. The reason that he's so expensive even at age 29 is because he's under contract through age 34. So I mean this is I'm going to talk about Garrett Wilson in a little bit. Garrett Wilson under contract for several more seasons, but he's younger. But if you acquire anybody, especially a star player with a lot of contract left, you're going to have to pay for that because typically a the contractual control is valuable, but the team who paid him the contract has already paid him out a big signing bonus and they're going to have to eat a lot of dead money because that's prrated over the portion of the contract for salary cap reasons, but has already been paid out by the original team. So to make it worth their while, you've got to fork over big draft capital. Aggressive aggressive move from the Chicago Bears. Now the timing on this move from the Bears, it almost feels scripted. The Seahawks just traded for Quentyn Nelson to better combat some of these interior rushers. He's a left guard on the offensive side. The Bears and the Seahawks play on Monday night in Seattle. So Jeffrey Simmons is going to join Chicago. I think he's going to bolster this defense. He's going to move the defense up on the XY chart. I think firmly makes the Bears contenders in this NFC. I'd already speculated that a Bears 49ers NFC title game was very possible, but on Monday night, Quentyn Nelson's going to have to block Jeffrey Simmons. And the 49ers, they're happy about that in the short term. That's for sure. They would like to maximize the chances of a Seattle loss in the short term to be able to best hold their lead. They've got a two and a half loss column game lead in the NFC West. But in the long term, you know, zoom out and look at 2027, 28, 29. Who's the biggest threat to the 49ers long term? San Francisco's got top shelf quarterback, right? And Brock Perie, he's going to be around for a while. Kyle Shanahan is going to be around for as long as he wants. The 49ers have proven that this is a sustainable build. I, you know, [snorts] everybody could talk about Mike McDonald and the Seahawks. That that's a defense driven team. The offense ranks in the 20s. I don't know if they're going to be legitimate contenders unless they can figure out how to make a perennial top 10 offense. And the Rams, I mean, the the book might be closing on them. the Chicago Bears with Ben Johnson and with Caleb Williams. These guys are I think going to be at the Thorn for a while. I I wouldn't be surprised if it's San Francisco and Chicago going at it in the NFC over the years. And now the Bears have themselves a defensive piece under contract for several seasons that they hope is going to help be the fortification so that this is a top half defense. You pair the top half defense with an elite offense. That's the goal. Now, back to the 49ers. Speaking of an elite offense, I was just in Nashville. We recorded this. Let's talk about the wide receiver position and some potential trades the 49ers can make in this arm race to bolster the receiver room. You got to believe that they're tempted to set themselves up for the long term at wide receiver. By that I mean the big prize, Garrett Wilson. Now I don't know if the Jets are willing to trade Garrett Wilson. And I think that's the big question mark. But the guy is still under team control for four seasons beyond this one through age 30. He's only 26 years old. First three seasons in the league, over a thousand yards receiving. And just look at the 49er structure here at wide receiver. And I'll also go to some less expensive options and we'll talk about all the guys coming back. That's all factors into what seems to be really complicated situation at receivers. So, nobody knows exactly what the 49ers will do. But consider the fact that Brandon Aayuk walked away from this team after they gave him a $120 million contract. That signifies that the 49ers are serious about investing big money in wide receiver with Brock Perie as their quarterback. That money obviously opened up when I left. So, then they signed Mike Evans. It was an upgrade over Aayuk in the short term, but obviously much older. And we know that Mike Evans is hobbled. I know he's under contract for three seasons. I don't know how long that's going to last though for the 49ers. It could only be a one season arrangement. He's awesome, but the 49ers do have to think about the longer term future as well. So, Evans also came at a discount to the 49ers. He didn't eat up all of that 30 million annually that Brandon Iayuk had eaten up before. So I I think there still definitely is money earmarked for the wide receiver position. And if you know, acquiring Garrett Wilson this year, if the Jets were willing to do it, obviously for a ton of draft capital would give the 49ers a receiver at less than five million this year because the Jets have already paid his signing and option bonus and 24.5 million guaranteed next season with team control all the way through age 30. So, couple more seasons even beyond that. You have to believe that financially for the 49ers it actually would be possible given the fact that that Evans money is manageable and it's not forever and may not even extend beyond this season. Mike Evans only had one year of guaranteed money. And then you think about what the setup would look like down the stretch run of this year. Evans, not a whole lot of pressure or not all the pressure on Mike Evans because Garrett Wilson would be there. George KD, Christian McAffrey, guys that could separate all across the field. I mean, Brock Perie theoretically behind the number one pass blocking offensive line in the NFL would have guys to throw to. You guys hear Savannah Lombardi here. I'm going to [crying] That is her. That is her excited about the 49ers potentially adding Garrett Wilson into the mix. Now, there potentially are options for the 49ers here at wide receiver who might be more attainable because I I don't know what the Jets are thinking, but Josh DS just requested a trade from the Indianapolis Colts. The issue with Josh DS is that he's a smaller receiver and we know that Perie, Brock Perie has paired better with taller receivers. However, DS is an elite separator. He gets open and he hadn't been used all that much with the Colts because they were thrown to guys like Alec Pierce instead. They also have Tyler Warren, a nice tight end over there in Indianapolis. But DS can separate and anybody who can separate, I think, could produce for your offense. On top of that, he's got punt return ability. And the 49ers are, I think, very clearly looking to upgrade over Jacob Cowing at punt returner. That could be a big boost because special teams is a part of this roster right now that has not been performing well. If you don't believe that the 49ers would try to go for a shorter receiver with Brock Birdie, look no further than one of his former teammates in college, Xavier Hutchinson, a 6-3 receiver, and this might be a really getable guy on the final year of his rookie deal. He plays for the Texans. The Texans aren't any good. Perie and Hutchinson had a great report Iowa State from 2020 to 2021. And I, you know, really believe that if you're looking for a costefficient addition that you might even be able to extend if you really like those tall receivers for Brock Birdie, somebody like Xavier Hutchinson might work. I've already expressed my doubts about Brian Thomas Jr. just given the fact that he's not working out in the Liam cone system in in Jacksonville and and that's a system that is going to have a lot of commonalities with what Kyle Shanahan is running. That's a McVey tree system and obviously we know that's related to to what the 49ers are doing, but he's out there as well. And so is Jawan Jennings, but I don't know if Jawan Jennings is out there and available for trade because the Minnesota Vikings, guess what? This is a 6 and0 football team and they're in competition with the 49ers to be the one seed in the NFC. Why would they try to help San Francisco out with a plug-and-play receiver? So, it might be one of those situations where the big swing, the massive swing for San Francisco is the one that actually makes most sense. Cable car making its way downhill. Couldn't have two more different environments, right? Driving down the old Natchas Trace in Tennessee where Jeffrey Simmons is coming from to Chicago to here San Francisco and the Bay Area. 49ers want to make sure that they host that upcoming NFC Championship game against the Bears. But wow, I the arms race just getting started. And you know, I said yesterday when we were out at the farm, I said, "Thank you to the Seahawks and the 49ers." Yesterday, they made us feel like it was the 1990s again. Remember that great arms race between the 49ers and the Cowboys just as the NFL was instituting the salary cap? Well, the NFC arms race is in full swing. And maybe this means that somebody like Khalil Mack is headed to the 49ers next.
